case_name: Real Canadian Superstore v. United Food and Commercial Workers, Local 1400
text:
1999
SKQB 196

Q.B.                                                                                                                              A.D.
1999

No. 603                                                                                                                                J.C.S.

IN
THE QUEEN’S BENCH

JUDICIAL
CENTRE OF SASKATOON

IN THE MATTER OF
AN APPLICATION PURSUANT TO

PART FIFTY-TWO
OF THE QUEEN’S BENCH RULES

AND

IN THE
MATTER OF AN APPLICATION FOR

JUDICIAL REVIEW
CONCERNING AN ARBITRATION AWARD

DATED
THE 18TH DAY OF JANUARY, 1999

BETWEEN:

THE REAL
CANADIAN SUPERSTORE,

(a division of
Westfair Foods Ltd.)

APPLICANT

-
and -

UNITED FOOD AND
COMMERCIAL WORKERS,

LOCAL 1400 and
AN ARBITRATION BOARD

CHAIRED BY
Merrilee Rasmussen, Q.C.

RESPONDENTS

Larry Seiferling, Q.C.                                                                              for
the applicant employer

Drew Plaxton                                                                                             for
the respondent union

JUDGMENT                                                                                                                  SMITH
J.

November
18, 1999

[
1
]                   This is one of two applications before me for
judicial review of an arbitration award.  The two cases involve two locals of
the same union, United Food and Commercial Workers, but different and unrelated
employers.  The employer in the instant case is the Real Canadian Superstore;
in the companion case it is Coca-Cola Bottling Ltd.  Both applications raise
the question of whether a bonus provision in a collective bargaining agreement,
of general application in the workplace, contravenes the prohibition in
s.
16(1)
of
The

Saskatchewan Human Rights Code,
S.S. 1979, c. S-24.1
against discrimination in the terms and conditions of employment on the basis
of disability.

[
2
]                   In the instant case, the employer seeks to quash
the interim award of an arbitration board chaired by Merrilee Rasmussen, Q.C.
(hereafter, the “Rasmussen Award”).  In the companion case it is the union that
seeks to quash the award of an arbitration board chaired by Susan Barber
(hereafter, the “Barber Award”.)  In both cases, the grievors were employees
who had been found ineligible, or only partially eligible, for a bonus provided
by the collective agreement to employees who were working during a specified
period or on a specified date.  The grievors in each case were absent on the
eligibility date (in one case) or during at least part of the eligibility
period (in the other) as a result of a leave of absence from their employment
due to an illness or accident.

[
3
]                   In both cases, the union argued, first, that the
collective agreements should not be interpreted as excluding or limiting these
employees’ eligibility for the bonuses provided, but  each of the arbitration
boards ruled against the union on that point.  No exception is taken to that
ruling in the instant application, although it is challenged in the companion
case, involving the employer, Coca-Cola Bottling Ltd. Alternatively, the union
argued in each case that if the collective agreements were so interpreted, the
boards should find that the eligibility requirements in the bonus provisions of
the respective collective agreements contravene
s. 16(1)
of
The
Saskatchewan
Human Rights Code

in that they discriminate in the terms and conditions of
employment on the basis of a disability.  On this issue, the union was
successful before the Rasmussen Board, in the instant matter, but unsuccessful
before the Barber Board.  The union argues that these two awards are
inconsistent in their respective interpretations of s. 16(1) of the
Code
.

[
4
]                   It is common ground that the standard of review on
the issue of the proper interpretation of the
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code

by a board of arbitration constituted under a collective bargaining agreement
is correctness, for this statute is external to the jurisdiction of the Board,
and outside its recognized area of expertise.

[
5
]                   While these two cases raise virtually the same
issue of interpretation of the discrimination prohibition in the
Code
,
and they were argued together before me, there are some distinctions between
collective agreement provisions at issue in the two matters, and the Coca-Cola
case involves broader issues.  Accordingly, although there will inevitably be
considerable overlap, comparison,  and repetition in the two judgments, I will
address the applications separately.

[
6
]                   The bonus provision at issue in the instant case is
in the Westfair Foods Collective Bargaining Agreement, a first collective
agreement between Superstore and the union, respecting the period from July 28,
1996, to July 24, 1999.  Appendix A of the agreement provides for bonus
payments of $475 to be paid on each of October 20, 1996, July 27, 1997, July
26, 1998 and July 25, 1999, “to each full time employee and prorated on hours
worked for part-time employees.”  Pro-rating of the bonus for part-time
employees was calculated in respect of the period January 1, 1996, to October
20, 1996, as a proportion of the hours a full-time employee would have worked in
this period.

[
7
]                   The grievor Brad Zdunich had been employed
part-time by the employer since July, 1991, his hours varying over time.  He
was injured in a
car accident on February 14, 1995 and was
not able to work at all as a result of his injuries until March 3, 1996.  Prior
to the accident he had worked
an average of 30 hours a week, compared to
full-time employment of 39 hours per week.  A bonus payment was made to Mr.
Zdunich in the December 28, 1996 pay period prorated for the hours he actually
worked during  the relevant 1996 period.  Thus, in making the calculation for
prorating his entitlement to the bonus, he did not receive credit for the hours
he would have worked prior to March 3, 1996, if he had not been physically
disabled by the injuries he received in the car accident.

[
8
]                   It is clear and undisputed that Mr. Zdunich’s
injuries resulting from the automobile accident constitute a “disability”
within the meaning of s. 2 of the
Code
.  The issue is whether prorating
his bonus entitlement to reflect his absence from work due to these injuries
constitutes “discrimination” within the meaning of s. 16(1).  The majority of
the board, (the employer nominee dissenting), found that “the application of
the calculation of the bonus provision on the basis of hours worked has
adversely affected the Grievor because of his disability that prevented him
from working,” and that this “adverse effect” constituted discrimination in the
terms and conditions of employment on the basis of disability, contrary to s.
16(1) of the
Code
.  It is this finding that is challenged by the
employer in the application before me.

[
9
]                   Section 16(1) provides as follows:

16(1) No employer shall refuse to employ or
continue to employ or otherwise discriminate against any person or class of
persons with respect to employment, or any term or condition of employment,
because of his or their race, creed, religion, colour, sex, sexual orientation,
family status, marital status, disability, age, nationality, ancestry, place of
origin or receipt of public assistance.

[
10
]                 It is clear that the impugned provision of the
collective bargaining agreement does not directly discriminate against the
grievor, or against persons with disabilities.  On its face it is a neutral
provision of general application.    In addition, the Rasmussen Board found
that in the proration of his entitlement to the bonus, on the basis of the
actual hours worked in 1996, the grievor  was treated in the same manner as
every other part-time employee in that “the prorating of all bonus payments to
part-time employees was based on actual hours worked by them during the
relevant period of time, regardless of the reason they did not work more
hours.”  The award pointed out, further, that other part-time employees who did
not work during this period but remained as employees included those on
maternity, paternity and adoption leave, holidays, illness, injury at or away
from work or because of restricted availability.

[
11
]                 In addition, there is no suggestion that Mr. Zdunich
was unjustifiably prevented from working his usual number of hours due to
employer discrimination, whether by failure to reasonably accommodate his
injuries or otherwise.  Mr. Zdunich was told by his supervisor that he would
receive seniority credits and other benefits provided to employees during the
period of time he was off work with his injuries.  His employment relationship
with the employer was not terminated and he did in fact receive seniority
credits.

[
12
]                 The Rasmussen Award held, nonetheless, that the
prorated calculation of the bonus to be paid to Mr. Zdunich, on the basis of
the hours he actually worked in comparison to full-time hours, constituted
discrimination in one of the terms and conditions of his employment because the
calculation was made “with reference to a criterion he cannot meet because of
his disability.”

[
13
]                 In its analysis, the Rasmussen Award pointed out that
human rights legislation is considered to have a “quasi-constitutional status”
and is therefore to be accorded a broad and liberal construction.  The Board
also noted that it is settled law that discrimination does not have to be
intentional to be prohibited, and that the courts have interpreted provisions
such as s. 16(1) as prohibiting not only direct discrimination but also “adverse
effect” discrimination that results when conduct apparently neutral on its face
has the effect of discriminating on a prohibited ground.  (Citing
Andrews v.
Law Society of British Columbia
,
1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 143
at 175
.)

[
14
]                 In its determination that the application of the
collective bargaining provision to the case of this grievor constitutes adverse
effect discrimination prohibited by s. 16(1) of the
Code
, the Rasmussen
Award began its analysis with the comment that, in relation to the prohibition
in this section against discrimination in respect of any term or condition of
employment, “there are no exceptions to this prohibition as may be found in
section 11 of the Ontario legislation.”  (This comment is a reference to an
express prohibition in the Ontario legislation against adverse effect
discrimination that is in turn expressly subject to a “bona fide occupational
requirement” (“BFOR”) defence.  The comment is relevant to a distinction the
Rasmussen Board sought to make in relation to the decision of the Ontario Court
of Appeal in
Ontario Nurses’ Association v. Orillia Soldiers Memorial
Hospital

(1999),
1999 CanLII 3687 (ON CA)
,
169 D.L.R. (4th) 489
,
42 O.R. (3d) 692
(a decision I
discuss more fully below).

This comment by the Board is amplified in
footnote 11 of the Award, at p. 10:

Subsection 16(7) [of
The

Saskatchewan
Human Rights Code
]

provides a limited exemption to allow
discrimination where ability is a “reasonable occupational qualification and
requirement for the position or employment”.  Subsection 16(7) has no
application to the circumstances of the present case, which is not about
discrimination in access to employment, but, rather, about discrimination in
the availability of a particular employment benefit.

This comment was apparently offered in support of the
Board’s view that the reasonableness of the rule or policy at issue is
irrelevant in determining whether it is discriminatory.

[
15
]                 The Board continued its analysis by noting that discrimination
“is fundamentally a comparison of the treatment of one group of employees to
another.”  Therefore, the first step in the analysis, to determine whether
there is discrimination in a particular case, “is to compare the treatment of
that employee to the treatment given to other employees, that is to some other
appropriate ‘comparator group’.” (At p. 10.)  In this regard, the award
acknowledged that the comparator group chosen may be determinative of the
outcome of the case and therefore the choice must be carefully made, on a
principled basis.  Referring to the decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada in

Brooks v. Canada Safeway Ltd.
,
1989 CanLII 96 (SCC)
,
[1989] 1 S.C.R. 1219
and
Gibbs v.
Battlefords & District Co-operative Ltd.,
1996 CanLII 187 (SCC)
,
[1997] 1 W.W.R. 1
, the Board
concluded that in order to determine the appropriate comparator group it must
first determine “what is the true character or underlying rationale of the
bonus provision of the collective agreement.” (At p. 12.)

[
16
]                 The Board then made the following finding:

The bonus provision is, in effect, a “signing” bonus.
As it says, it is payable to all employees.
Its purpose is to provide a
lump sum cash payment to persons who are employees, without affecting wage
scales or “end lift”.
That is, employees are effectively provided a small
raise in pay in a year without committing the employer to continuing to pay the
raise in subsequent years. . . . (At p. 12, emphasis added.)

[
17
]                 This finding is significant, and I shall return to
it, for it supports the conclusion that the purpose, or underlying rationale,
of the signing bonus is to provide to employees, on a short-term basis,
additional compensation, or wages, in a way that does not affect wage scales in
future years.

[
18
]                 From this point in the award, the Board’s analysis is
somewhat unclear.  Having addressed the difference in the treatment of
full-time and part-time employees in relation to bonus entitlement, (full-time
employees were to receive the bonus without regard to the number of hours
actually worked during the relevant periods while the entitlement of part-time
employees was to be prorated, as described) the conclusion of the Board with
respect to the issue of the appropriate “comparator group” is apparently
contained in this sentence:

. . . It is
in this context of his status as a
part-time employee
that it must be determined whether the Grievor’s absence
from the workplace due to disability ought to disentitle him to
a bonus
calculated on the hours he would have worked but for the disability.
(At p.
15, emphasis added.)

[
19
]                 Thus, the Board apparently determined that the
appropriate comparator group in this instance is the group of all part-time
employees.  This conclusion seems correct, and in accordance with the
rationale, or underlying purpose, of the bonus provision, as found by the
Board.  However, strangely, the Board did not continue the analysis, at this
point, to ask whether there has been differential treatment between the grievor
and other part-time employees, as a result of his disability.  Had it done so,
its answer, in my view, could only have been that there has not.  It is clear
from
the decisions in
Brooks
and
Gibbs
that whether there is
disparate treatment on a prohibited basis must also be determined in relation
to the underlying rationale of the rule, policy or benefit at issue.   The
grievor’s entitlement to a bonus for the period in question, like that of all
other part-time employees, was pro-rated on the basis of the hours actually
worked during the relevant period, in comparison with full-time hours.  In
relation to the treatment of the hours he had not worked as a result of his
disability leave, he was treated the same as all other part-time workers who
had been on leave or absent from their usual hours of work.  The correlation
between hours actually worked (by the grievor as well as all other part-time
employees) and entitlement to bonus is rationally related to the underlying
purpose of the bonus provision to provide a short-term increase in wages, or
compensation for work performed, payable to employees.  Thus, while it is true,
as the Board noted, that the grievor’s
disability
had an “adverse
effect” upon his entitlement to the bonus, it is wrong to conclude that such
effect was
disparate
in comparison with the effect of the policy on
other members of the comparator group  and was therefore discriminatory.

[
20
]                 Indeed, payment of the bonus to this grievor on the
basis required by the Rasmussen Award would require that he be compensated, by
way of the bonus provision, for work he did not perform, resulting in more
favourable

treatment for the grievor than for other members of the comparator group, (all
other part-time employees) whose bonus entitlement was prorated on the basis of
actual hours worked.

[
21
]                 The question of whether there has been
differential

treatment, in relation to the comparator group, is crucial, on the analysis
commenced by the Board, for without it there is no basis for finding
discrimination
,
direct or constructive.  That is, on the analysis undertaken by the Board, it
was necessary to find disparate treatment--that the grievor was treated less
favourably than others in the comparator group to whom the rule applied.  As I
have indicated, this is clear from the cases upon which the Board relied.

[
22
]
In
Gibbs
,
supra
, Sopinka J., writing
for the majority, described the principles to be applied in this analysis,
emphasizing the importance of considering the underlying purpose, or rationale,
of a benefit in order to determine whether the treatment of the complainant was
discriminatory, in comparison with other members of the comparator group.
After some discussion of the Court’s earlier
decision in
Brooks
,
supra
,
he commented:

. . . That is, since the insurance
in
Brooks

was intended to compensate those absent from work for health-related
reasons, the relevant comparison was between the benefits available to pregnant
employees and those available to employees unable to work for other health
reasons.

In my view,
Brooks
, supra
, provides

a useful guide in determining the appropriate group to compare to mentally
disabled employees in the case at bar.  The first step is to determine, in all
the circumstances of the case, the purpose of the disability plan.  Comparing
the benefits allocated to employees pursuant to different purposes is not
helpful in determining discrimination—it is understandable that insurance
benefits designed for disparate purposes will differ.
If, however, benefits
are allocated pursuant to the same purpose, yet benefits differ as the result
of characteristics that are not relevant to this purpose, discrimination may
well exist
. (At pp. 17-18, emphasis added.)

[
23
]                 There are cases, of course, in which courts have held
that a neutral rule or policy of general application has disparate
discriminatory effect because, on analysis, it is shown to have a
disproportionate impact on a particular group, identified by a prohibited
ground.  This was the finding, for example, in the leading American case on
this point,
Griggs v. Duke Power Co.,
401 U.S. 424 (1971), frequently
cited with approval by the Supreme Court of Canada (see, for example,
Ontario
Human Rights Commission and O’Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Limited
,
1985 CanLII 18 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2
S.C.R. 536
at 550)
.  In that case, the Supreme Court of the United States found
a requirement for a high school diploma for employment or advancement in
employment discriminatory even though it applied equally to all employees,
because it had the effect of excluding from employment a much higher proportion
of black applicants than white.  It was found that the requirement was not
related to performance on the job and the Supreme Court of the United States
held the requirement to be discriminatory because of its disproportionate
effect upon the black population.

[
24
]                 It was apparently not argued, however, and certainly
there was no finding by the Rasmussen Board, that the bonus eligibility
requirement in the instant case had a disproportionate adverse effect on
disabled employees.  Nor, as I have indicated, was there a finding that basing
eligibility on hours actually worked was unrelated to the purpose of the bonus
provision.

[
25
]                 Rather than make a finding of disparate
discriminatory effect of the application of the bonus provision in comparison
with other members of an appropriately determined comparator group, what the
Board appears to have done is to switch, at this point in its award, to a
completely different logical analysis, having nothing to do with comparator
groups, to argue that the grievor suffered an “adverse effect”, in relation to
the bonus provided, because he received a lower bonus, as a result of his
disability,
than he would have received but for his disability.
This
argument is clearly based upon the application of a simple “but for” test:
i.e., has the grievor been treated less favourably by the application of this
policy than he would have been but for his disability?  Application of this
test, however, does not require a comparison between the grievor’s treatment
and that of all other part-time employees, or any other members of a comparator
group.  Rather, the comparison drawn is between the grievor’s entitlement to
bonus on application of the rule and what he would have received, on
application of the same rule,
but for his disability
.

[
26
]                 The same logic is reflected in the following passage,
in which the Rasmussen Board rejected the argument accepted by the Barber
Board, in what is now the companion case before me:

. . . Arbitrator Barber held that a
provision in a collective agreement that required the payment of a bonus to
“regular full-time employees” who were “actively at work” effective January 1
was not discriminatory because five employees who were on long term disability
at that time did not receive the bonus.  She held that the loss of the benefit
was not triggered by disability, but by the failure to be actively at work.
With respect, this analysis fails to appreciate the character of adverse effect
discrimination.  If an employee does not receive a benefit that other employees
receive because he or she is disabled, it is no answer to say that others who
were absent from work who were not disabled also did not receive the benefit.
Clearly, the others who did not receive the benefit, did not receive it for
reasons that are not discriminatory.  To say these other employees were not
discriminated against says nothing about the treatment received by those
employees who were disabled.  This point is well-illustrated by Arbitrator
Barber’s own rhetorical question:  “What if all of them [employees who did not
receive the bonus] happened to be aboriginal and ineligible to receive the
bonus because of leave for educational purposes.  Would that amount to
discrimination because of race?”  Ineligibility in this example is not
triggered by race; it is triggered by absence on educational leave.  It cannot
be said that “but for” their race, these employees would have received a bonus.
. . . (At p. 16.)

[
27
]                 This analysis is, in my view, clearly
contrary to the
approach described in
Gibbs

and
Brooks
, and much of the
discussion in those cases relating to the underlying rationale of the benefit
and determination of the appropriate group for comparison would be irrelevant
if the appropriate test for determining adverse effect discrimination were a
simple “but for” test.

[
28
]                 The Rasmussen Board’s conclusion that “adverse effect
discrimination” is to be determined on the basis of a simple “but for” test was
seen, even by the Board itself, to have very far-reaching consequences,
particularly in light of the fact that the Board, having noted that s. 16(7) of
the
Code
does not provide a BFOR defence where there is employer
discrimination in relation to the terms and conditions of employment,
apparently concluded that the underlying purpose or rationale of the term or
condition of employment at issue is therefore
irrelevant
.  The following
passage from the award is instructive in this regard:

The Employer has strenuously argued that
distinctions based on hours worked can’t possibly be discriminatory.  If they
are, the argument continues, employers would then be compelled to hire disabled
persons and, once they were employees, would be compelled to pay them for not
working.  The Board agrees that such consequences cannot have been the result
intended by the inclusion in
The
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code
of a
prohibition against discrimination in employment on the grounds of disability.
Nor would they be the result.  Subsection 16(7) of the Code permits employers
to discriminate on the basis of ability “where. . .ability. . .is a reasonable
occupational requirement for the position or employment.”  It seems obvious
that the ability to do the job would be a “reasonable occupational requirement”
that an employer could insist upon, even if such insistence adversely affected
disabled persons.
However, no such relaxation of the prohibition against
discrimination on the basis of disability exists in relation to the treatment
by employers of persons who are employees.  The fact of the matter is that if
any terms or conditions of employment adversely affect disabled employees by
reason of their being disabled, they are discriminatory
.  (At p. 15,
emphasis added.)

[
29
]                 It is clear that, on the Board’s analysis, any denial
of or limitation to a benefit that an employee, once employed, would have
received “but for” his or her disability constitutes discrimination within the
meaning of the
Code
, is prohibited by s. 16(1), and is not subject to
the “bona fide occupational requirement” (“BFOR”) defence provided by s. 16(7).

[
30
]                In my view, the employer was right in suggesting, in
the passage quoted, that this very stringent interpretation of s. 16(1) leads
to consequences that could not have been intended by the legislation, and that
the Board’s response does not adequately address this point.  Most obviously,
for example, if the Board’s analysis were correct, the same argument that
compels payment of the bonus at issue to the grievor, on the basis of the hours
he would have worked had he not been injured, would equally compel payment of
regular wages to him for the time he was unable to work as a result of his
injuries, on the same basis, with the result that he would, in effect, receive
full compensation for work that he was unable to perform.

[
31
]                 This consequence is by no means limited to the
grievor’s particular case.  It is now clear that regardless of the BFOR defence
contained in s. 16(7), and despite the absence in the Saskatchewan legislation
of any express duty to accommodate, the
Code
is to be interpreted as
imposing on an employer, in decisions involving hiring or promotion, (i.e.
access to or participation in the workplace) a duty to accommodate the special
needs of disabled employees (or employees in other protected groups) to the
point of undue hardship.  See, for example, the decisions of the Supreme Court
of Canada in the
O’Malley
case,
supra
, and in
Central Alberta
Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission)
,
1990 CanLII 76 (SCC)
,
[1990] 2 S.C.R. 489
.  This
duty could well result in the accommodation of a disabled employee by creating,
for example, a special part-time position in place of a full-time position to
accommodate an employee whose disability prevented her from working full time.
On the Board’s simple “but for” analysis, having made such an accommodation in
hiring the employee, it would then be discriminatory for the employer to pay
this employee less than full-time wages, if she would have been able to work
full time but for her disability.

[
32
]                 In short, the Board erred, in my view, in its
reliance on a  simple “but for” test to conclude that the grievor suffered
“adverse effect discrimination”.  Generally, to find that a rule or policy of
general application, neutral on its face, has a
discriminatory
adverse
impact on an individual or group identified by a protected ground, it is
necessary to find
disparate
treatment of the individual or group in
comparison to other members of the comparator group not so identified,
on
the basis of
the protected personal characteristic. In my view, it is not
possible to make that finding in this case.  Again, were it sufficient, in
order to find discrimination in the prohibited sense, to find simply that an
employee has received less benefit than he or she would have received had he or
she not been disabled, there would be no need for even entering into the
complex determination of the appropriate comparator group, based upon the
underlying purpose or rationale of the policy or rule at issue.  On the simple
“but for” test these factors, endorsed and relied upon in repeated decisions of
the Supreme Court, simply do not figure in the equation.

[
33
]                 The Board’s confusion in this case is attributable, I
believe, to a more general and widely prevalent confusion and uncertainty in
relation to the scope of the “duty to accommodate” the special needs of
protected groups that arbitrators, human rights commissions and the courts
have, generally, implied into both legislated protection against discrimination
and the guarantee of equality in s. 15 of the
Charter
.  In particular,
the Board has, in my view, failed to give effect to a distinction that must be
drawn between the duty imposed on employers to accommodate differences in order
to facilitate equal access to or participation in the workplace for individuals
and groups who may be excluded by reason of sex, religion or disability, for
example, and the prohibition against discriminatory
disparate
treatment
in relation to compensatory benefits provided for work performed.

[
34
]                 The Supreme Court’s view of the scope of the duty to
accommodate the differences of individuals and groups who have historically
been excluded from full participation in society, and its relation to duties
and defences expressly set out in various examples of equality legislation and
in s. 15 of the
Charter
has evolved over a series of cases, including
O’Malley
,

supra;

Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Borough of Etobicoke
,

1982 CanLII 15 (SCC)
,
[1982] 1 S.C.R. 202
;
Bhinder v. Canadian National Railway Company,

1985 CanLII 19 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 561
;
Brossard (Town) v. Quebec,

1988 CanLII 7 (SCC)
,
[1988] 2 S.C.R. 279
;
Brooks
supra
;
Saskatchewan (Human Rights Commission) v. Saskatoon (City)
,

1989 CanLII 18 (SCC)
,
[1989] 2 S.C.R. 1297
;
Alberta Human Rights Commission v. Central Alberta
Dairy Pool
,
1990 CanLII 76 (SCC)
,
[1990] 2 S.C.R. 489
;
Commission Scolaire Régionale de
Chambly v. Bergevin,
1994 CanLII 102 (SCC)
,
[1994] 2 S.C.R. 525
;
Eaton v. Brant County Board
of Education,
1997 CanLII 366 (SCC)
,
[1997] 1 S.C.R. 241
;
Gibbs
,
supra
;
Eldridge
v. British Columbia

(Attorney General)

(1997),
1997 CanLII 327 (SCC)
,
151 D.L.R. (4th) 577
(B.C.S.C.)
; and
British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations
Commission) v. British Columbia Government and Service Employees’ Union
(B.C.G.S.E.U.)
(1999),
1999 CanLII 652 (SCC)
,
176 D.L.R. (4th) 1 (S.C.C.)
.

[
35
]

It would be fair to say, on a review of these
cases, that there is no simple calculus available to determine the scope or
content of this duty, which has evolved and changed over fourteen years of
judicial interpretation since the implementation of s. 15 of the
Charter
,
and which is clearly driven, to a large extent, by policy considerations which,
in turn, drive a purposive interpretation of the
Charter
and, by
analogy, provincial and federal human rights statutes.  It is helpful, however,
to make special note of the recent comments of
the Supreme Court in
Eaton v.
Brant County Board of Education
,
supra
, in relation to the
interpretation of s. 15 of the
Charter
.
In
Eaton
the Court was
considering a claim by parents of a severely disabled child that she should be
included in the regular classrooms of the defendant’s schools.  In reflecting
on these issues, Sopinka J. offered the following distinction between two
equally important objectives of s. 15 of the
Charter
and, by
implication, also of legislated equality protections:

The principal object of
certain of the prohibited grounds is the elimination of discrimination by the
attribution of untrue characteristics based on stereotypical attitudes relating
to immutable conditions such as race or sex.  In the case of disability, this
is one of the objectives.
The other equally important objective seeks to
take into account the true characteristics of this group which act as headwinds
to the enjoyment of society’s benefits and to accommodate them.  Exclusion from
the mainstream of society results from the construction of a society based
solely on “mainstream” attributes to which disabled persons will never be able
to gain access.
Whether it is the impossibility of success at a written
test for a blind person, or the need for ramp access to a library, the
discrimination does not lie in the attribution of untrue characteristics to the
disabled individual.  The blind person cannot see and the person in a
wheelchair needs a ramp.  Rather, it is the failure to make reasonable
accommodation, to fine-tune society so that its structures and assumptions
do
not result in the relegation and banishment of disabled persons from
participation,
which results in discrimination against them.  The
discrimination inquiry which uses “the attribution of stereotypical
characteristics” reasoning as commonly understood is simply inappropriate here.
. . . (At pp. 272-73.)

[
36
]                 It is well established that human rights legislation
must be interpreted in light of the objectives reflected in the
Charter
.
What the comments of Sopinka J. make clear is that, while as a general rule the

Charter
and such legislation prohibit
disparate
treatment of
individuals on the basis of a protected ground, in some circumstances,
and
on a somewhat different rationale
, the prohibition against discrimination
compels

different or special treatment that recognizes the special needs of
disadvantaged individuals, especially those belonging to groups who have
historically been excluded from full participation in society.

[
37
]                 In “Human Rights in Employment: Of Participation and
Compensation”,  4 C.L.E.L.J. 283, Richard Brown made these comments about the
special importance of participation issues in the workplace:

The issue before the Supreme
Court in both
O’Malley
and
Central Alberta Dairy Pool
was one of
participation rather than compensation.  Participation was also the subject of
the comments of the Royal Commission about accommodating differences in the
pursuit of equality.  The Court and the Commission had very good reasons for
advocating sweeping legal protection of a person’s right to participate in the
workplace.  Taking part in the working world, and the particular part one
takes, have major financial consequences for individuals and add social and
psychological meaning to their lives.  The crucial importance of all of these
aspects of employment was acknowledged by Dickson C.J. in a case involving a
Charter

challenge to a ban on strikes:

In the present case, however, we are
concerned with interests which go far beyond those of a merely pecuniary
nature.

Work is one of the most fundamental
aspects in a person’s life, providing the individual with a means of financial
support and, as importantly, a contributory role in society.  A person’s
employment is an essential component of his or her sense of identity,
self-worth and emotional well-being.  Accordingly, the conditions in which a
person works are highly significant in shaping the whole compendium of
psychological, emotional and physical elements of a person’s dignity and self
respect.  [
Reference re Public Service Employee Relations Act (Alberta)
,

1987 CanLII 88 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R. 313
,
87 C.L.L.C. 14
,021 at 12,180.

Discrimination which precludes or restricts
access to the workplace reduces the victim’s enjoyment of the financial, social
and psychological rewards of employment.  Losing a job or promotion through
discrimination carries all of the costs entailed in losing one through
redundancy or any other cause.   This is true whether the discrimination is
direct or indirect.  The valuable advantages of employment are lost in a case
of indirect discrimination, where an employee is dismissed for refusing to work
on her sabbath, no less than in a case of direct discrimination, where she is
discharged solely because of animosity towards members of her religion.  In the
context of access, the similarity of direct and indirect discrimination in
their impact on the aggrieved individual explains why the law regulates both.
The benefits of participation in the workforce should not be distributed
according to any prohibited ground of discrimination, unless there are
compelling reasons to the contrary. (At pp. 286-87.)

[
38
]                 For reasons so well expressed by Chief Justice
Dickson, in the passage quoted by Brown, above, the duty to accommodate the
special needs of individuals, arising out of their membership in historically
excluded groups, in employment policies and decisions relating to participation
in the workplace clearly fall into this rationale.  It is for this reason that
human rights commissions and arbitrators, as well as the courts, have had no
difficulty reading into human rights legislation a duty on employers (and unions)
to accommodate to the point of undue hardship the special needs of disabled
employees in the context of employment practices relating to hiring and
promotion determinations, even where, as in the Saskatchewan legislation, no
such duty is expressly set out in the legislation, and regardless of any “BFOR”
defence, such as s. 16(7) of the Saskatchewan
Code
, provided by the
legislation.

[
39
]                 The determination of when this particular duty
arises, however, is necessarily subject to a logical analysis that differs from
that relevant to determination of discrimination based upon
disparate

treatment on a prohibited ground, in relation to the appropriate comparisons to
be drawn.  In order to determine whether a duty to accommodate access or
participation in employment arises, it is sufficient to ask whether the
individual’s inability to meet the generally applicable criteria for
participation arises in relation to a protected ground, such as disability.
For this purpose the “but for” test is an appropriate analytic tool, for it is
sufficient to ask, of a particular individual, whether he or she would qualify
for a position, promotion, or other opportunity to work, but for the
disability.  If the answer is yes, then there is a duty on the employer to make
reasonable adjustments to accommodate the disability, to the point of undue
hardship.  There is no need, in this particular context, to identify a
“comparator group” or to ask whether the claimant is being treated
differently

from other members of such a group, for the whole point is that
equal

treatment, in the context of rules or policies that affect participation, is
itself discriminatory by being exclusory of those with special needs.
Alternatively, it might be said that, in relation to issues of access and
participation in the workplace, the appropriate comparison is
always

between those who are, for example, disabled, and those who are not.  The “but
for” test generally accomplishes this comparison by comparing the treatment of
a disabled individual to the way he or she would be treated, but for his or her
disability.

[
40
]                 The result is that the simple “but for” analysis that
appears to lead to absurd and unintended results when the workplace issue is
compensation, generally works effectively in relation to issues of access and
participation.

[
41
]                 While one can certainly conceive of a social policy
that carries this particular principle of accommodation beyond issues of
participation to issues of compensation, for example, it is not, in my view,
reasonable to interpret the provisions of
The
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code

that are before me as if they were intended to reflect such a policy.  I have
already commented on the far-reaching consequences of applying such a logic.
Certainly the decisions of
the Supreme Court of Canada in
Brooks
, Chambly,
and

Gibbs
, all decisions dealing with allegations of discrimination in
relation to employment benefits, and all calling for determination of an
appropriate comparator group of other employees in light of the purpose of the
benefit at issue in order to make a finding of adverse discriminatory effect,
do not mandate such an interpretation.  To do so would imply that the
legislation at issue reflects an intention to place on individual employers the
responsibility, not only of making adjustments to the workplace to accommodate
the special needs of disabled persons to participate, as much as is reasonably
possible, in the workplace, but also the responsibility to make up any
resulting shortfall in employment benefits including compensation, or wages to
such employees when such accommodation proves limited or impossible.  I do not
believe that this legislative intention can be found.

[
42
]                 As Richard Brown,
supra
, commented:

. . . The denial of benefits to employees
off work for a prolonged period, including those on disability or pregnancy and
parental leave, rests on the notion that entitlement to compensation flows from
the performance of work, not on any belief that some people have greater
intrinsic worth than others, irrespective of their relative contribution in the
workplace.  (At pp. 304-05.)

[
43
]                 The Rasmussen Award itself, and the parties before
me, referred to two lines of arbitral authority, divided on the issue of
whether the duty of an employer to accommodate disabled employees in the
workplace applies only in relation to access to, or participation in, the
workplace, or, applies also in relation to the provision of compensatory
benefits to employees.  (There is no question, of course, but that direct
discrimination in relation to compensatory benefits on a prohibited ground
would contravene provincial equality legislation as well as s. 15 of the
Charter

in cases where it applies.)  One line of authority essentially applies the same
analysis reflected in the Rasmussen Award to finds a duty to accommodate, based
on the “but for” test, in both respects. The other distinguishes rules or
policies that relate to access to or participation in the workplace from rules
or policies providing compensatory benefits for work performed.

[
44
]                 The leading arbitration decision in the latter camp
is
Versa Services Ltd. and Milk and Bread Drivers, Dairy Employees, Caterers
and Allied Employees Union, Local 647, Re

(1994),
1994 CanLII 18586 (ON LA)
,
39 L.A.C. (4th) 196
, a
decision applied more recently in
Re Soldiers Memorial Hospital, Orillia and
Sault Ste. Marie General Hospital and Ontario Nurses’ Association

(1996),

1996 CanLII 20329 (ON LA)
,
58 L.A.C. (4th) 72
.  The latter decision was the subject of a recent judgment
in the Ontario Court of Appeal.
See
Ontario Nurses’ Association v. Orillia
Soldiers Memorial Hospital
, supra
.

[
45
]                 In
Versa Services
, Arbitrator R. M. Brown was
faced with a provision in the collective agreement requiring employees
collecting long-term disability (“LTD”) benefits to contribute more to the cost
of health and welfare benefits than those on the job.  The union argued that
this provision contravened the prohibition against discrimination on the ground
of a handicap found in the
Ontario Human Rights Code.
Sections 11(1)
and 17 of that
Code
provided as follows:

11(1)  A right of a person under Part I [the right
to equal treatment without discrimination because of an enumerated ground,
including “handicap”] is infringed where a requirement, qualification or factor
exists that is not discrimination on a prohibited ground but that results in
the exclusion, restriction or preference of a group of person who are
identified by a prohibited ground of discrimination and of whom the person is a
member, except where,

(a)      the requirement,
qualification or factor is reasonable and
bona fide
in the circumstances
. . .

. . .

17(1) A right of a person under this Act is not
infringed for the reason only that the person is incapable of performing or
fulfilling the essential duties or requirements attending the exercise of the
right because of handicap.

(2) The Commission, a board of inquiry or a court
shall not find a person incapable unless it is satisfied that the needs of the
person cannot be accommodated without undue hardship on the person responsible
for accommodating those needs, considering the cost, outside sources of
funding, if any, and health and safety requirements, if any.

[
46
]                 Thus, s. 11(1) of the Ontario legislation expressly
recognized that adverse discriminatory effect may arise from a rule or policy
that is neutral on its face, and s. 17 of the
Code
expressly provided a
general BFOR defence, coupled, in ss. (2), with a duty to accommodate the
special needs of disabled employees to facilitate their equal participation in
the workplace.   As I have indicated, above, it is clear that the same
principles reflected in these provisions also arise under the Saskatchewan
legislation, even though they are not expressly set out, for the courts have
interpreted more general legislative provisions, aimed at protecting and
enhancing equality, as implicitly prohibiting adverse effect discrimination and
as raising a duty to accommodate the special needs of protected groups to the
point of undue hardship.

[
47
]                 On a review of the evidence before him the arbitrator
indicated that he could not find that employees collecting LTD benefits were
being treated worse than other employees without a handicap who had a similar
attendance record.  He commented:

. . . I must assume entitlement to benefit
contributions turns on attendance at work, not on handicap.  In other words,
everyone is treated the same way, based upon attendance, regardless of
handicap. . . . (At p. 201.)

[
48
]                 Although he did not articulate every step in the
analysis, I interpret this passage as a finding by the arbitrator that the
provision of the collective agreement at issue does not constitute adverse
effect discrimination against disabled employees because they have not suffered
a disparate impact in comparison with other members of the workforce.  It is
important to note that he did not conclude that adverse effect discrimination
cannot

occur in relation to issues of compensation in the workplace.  He simply
concluded that it did not occur in this case.

[
49
]                 He then turned to consider whether, nonetheless, a
broader concept of equality inherent in the Ontario
Code
provisions
quoted above might place a greater obligation on an employer to accommodate the
differences of handicapped workers who work less because of their disability,
by providing
greater
benefits to them than to employees working the same
amount.  His reasoning in the following passage is instructive:

To some extent at least, the notion of
equal treatment embodied in the
Human Rights Code
requires employers to
do more than treat everyone the same without regard to handicap.  Section 17
requires employers to accommodate handicapped people by taking special measures
to allow them access to employment.  Consider a person whose handicap prevents
her from operating a machine as it presently exists, but who could operate the
machine if it were modified in a manner which would not impose an undue hardship
on the employer.  To refuse to employ this person as a machine operator because
of her disability would be a violation of the Code.  The employer is not
permitted to exclude this individual from employment by treating her in the
same way as an able-bodied person who is required to operate the machine in its
unmodified form.  As well as requiring an employer to modify the work
environment, the duty to accommodate also may require an employer to grant
unpaid leave to someone whose disability temporarily prevents her from
working.  In these ways, people with a handicap must be accommodated by taking
special measures to allow them to participate in the working world, so long as
doing so does not entail undue expense for the employers concerned.

The case at hand is not about modifying jobs so
they can be performed by disabled people.  It is not about entering or leaving
the world of work.  The handicaps afflicting employees on LTD benefits are
sufficiently serious that they are unable to work for more than a year.  The
union contends the employer is obliged to make benefit contributions on their
behalf while they are off the job.  As these contributions are a form of
compensation, this case concerns compensation while not working, rather than
participation in the world of work.  According to the union, the Code compels
the employer to bear the cost of providing benefits to these employees, even
though benefits are not provided to able-bodied employees who are absent from
work for such a prolonged period.  Does equal treatment require not only
accommodative measures to allow people to work, but also special payments for
those unable to do so?

I think not.  In my view, the Code treats
compensation differently from participation.  The reference in s. 17 to a
person’s capability to perform duties indicates this section applies to
engagement in active employment.  On this front, s. 17 adopts the broader
notion of equal treatment which requires differences to be accommodated, so as
not to exclude a handicapped person from a work place.  Section 17 cannot be
construed as applying the same broad notion of equal treatment to compensation
because it contains no reference to compensation.  There is no other section of
the Code which specifically applies this broader understanding of equality,
which requires special measures, to compensation for handicapped employees.  I
believe the absence of such a section indicates a legislative intention to
apply a different understanding of equality to matters of compensation.  A
handicapped person’s only entitlement is to be compensated in the same way as
someone without a handicap.  If employees without a handicap receive
compensation during short absences, so too must those with a disability.
Conversely, if most employees receive no compensation during prolonged
absences, those with a handicap have no complaint when they are treated in the
same way.

In coming to this conclusion, I have not
overlooked s. 11 of the Code which adopts a broad understanding of equal
treatment.  Section 11 renders unlawful a rule or practice which results in
members of a protected group being disadvantaged relative to others, even
though members of this group are treated the same as everyone else.  An example
of an offending rule is one excluding from employment people below a certain
height, which has the effect of barring a larger percentage of female
applicants than of male applicants, because women on average are shorter than
men.  As handicapped employees are more likely than others to have prolonged
absences from work, can it be argued that s. 11 requires an employer to make
benefits contributions for employees with a long-term disability, even though
no contributions are made for those absent from work for the same length of
time for other reasons?  This argument is more persuasive when s. 11 is viewed
in isolation than when it is seen against the backdrop of s. 17.  Section 17 is
addressed exclusively to handicap.  This section requires special treatment to
enable people with disabilities to participate in active employment, but stops
short of requiring special compensation measures.  This deliberate omission in
a section dealing specifically with handicap should not be negated by a broad
reading of the more general requirements of s. 11 which addresses all of the
prohibited grounds of discrimination.

My confidence in this interpretation of the statute
is bolstered by sound policy reasons for treating participation and
compensation differently.  The basic reason for requiring an employer to take
accommodative measures to allow people with handicaps to engage in active
employment is that management has control over the work place.  An employer is
the only one who can make the necessary changes to its plant or office.  While
it is possible to reimburse an employer for the associated expense, the law
cannot protect the right to participate in the world of work without requiring
specific employers to accommodate people with disabilities.  (For similar
reasons, the law cannot protect the right to participate in other spheres of
community life without requiring specific providers of goods and services to
take special measures.)  In contrast, financial assistance can be made
available to a disabled person without requiring any particular employer to
bear the cost.  Moreover, there are good reasons for spreading the cost of
monetary assistance to a handicapped person across employers or taxpayers in
general, rather than placing it on any particular employer.  Financial
assistance is provided through such cost-spreading programs as social
assistance and workers’ compensation at the provincial level and unemployment
insurance and Canada Pension Plan at the federal level.  These statutory
programs address the financial needs of people with disabilities.  While the
Human
Rights Code
requires special measures to enable handicapped people to
participate in the life of the community, the code does not entitle them to
extraordinary forms of compensation not available to other employees absent
from work.

[
50
]                 With respect, it is my view that this approach and
the distinction drawn by the arbitrator in
Versa Services
between the
duty, on the one hand, to accommodate the special needs of disabled workers to
facilitate full and equal participation in the workplace, (which goes beyond
the requirement of equal treatment), and the duty on the other hand to
accommodate differences that arise out of a finding of disparate treatment, is
sound.

[
51
]                 In the
Orillia Hospital
case the arbitrator
had dealt with the application of  provisions of a collective agreement
relating to accrual of seniority and service and employer contribution to
subsidized benefit plans to nurses on long-term disability leave.  In effect,
while nurses on unpaid leave, including those on disability leave, remained
employees, they did not accumulate seniority and service after a period of time
set out in the agreement, and the employer was not required to contribute
premiums to benefit plans after the nurses had been receiving long-term
disability payments for specified periods of time. The arbitration board,
purporting to follow the
Versa Services
decision, determined, as a
matter of policy that required balancing of interests to determine the scope of
an employer’s duty to accommodate, that reduction of compensatory benefits
(service accrual and employer contribution to subsidized benefit plans)
could
not
be considered adverse effect discrimination within the meaning of s. 11
of the Ontario
Code
.  It held that limitation of the accrual of
seniority, on the other hand, had the effect of limiting the ability of
disabled persons to participate equally in the workplace, and therefore did
contravene the
Code
.

[
52
]                 The Ontario Court of Appeal rejected the arbitrator’s
suggestion that there could not, as a matter of policy, be adverse effect
discrimination within the meaning of s. 11 in relation to issues of
compensation in the workplace.  With respect, this seems to be correct.  It
accords with the analysis of discrimination set out by
the Supreme Court of
Canada in
Gibbs
, supra
, and with the decision of the Supreme Court in
Chambly,
supra.
In the latter case, the Court held, on a comparative analysis, that
a school calendar that recognized major Christian holidays and provided leave
with pay on such days to all teachers, while neutral on its face, constituted
adverse effect discrimination against a Jewish teacher, who was required to
take a day off without pay in order to celebrate Yom Kippur.  The employer was
required to accommodate the teacher by providing a day of leave with pay for
the Jewish holiday.  The issue in this case clearly related to discrimination
in the provision of employment benefits, not in relation to participation in
the workplace. The
Versa Services
decision, upon which the
Orillia

arbitrator purported to rely, had, in my view, followed this line of authority
by determining, first, that the policy at issue in that case did not have an
adverse discriminatory effect on the disabled employees.

[
53
]                 The Court in
Orillia
went on to uphold the
distinction between compensation issues and participation issues in the
workplace, adopting much of the reasoning of Arbitrator Brown in
Versa
Services
, holding that the duty to accommodate contemplated by s. 11(1) of
the Ontario legislation does not include the duty simply to top up the wages or
other compensatory benefits of disabled employees, to compensate them as if
they were working when, as a result of a disability, they were unable to do
so.  Rosenberg J.A. commented:

. . . I do not read s. 11(2) as imposing
upon the employer the burden of simply topping up the wages of the disabled
employees.  That, in my view, is not the type of accommodation contemplated by
s. 11(2) and in fact is inimical to the principles underlying the Code. . . .
(At para. 54.)

. . .

Simply topping up the wages of the disabled
employees and paying them as if they are not disabled is nothing more than
reverse stereotyping. . . .Rather, it would seem to me that the employer in
this hypothetical must attempt to accommodate the group. For example, the
employer may provide devices and instruments that would allow the disabled employees
to perform close to the same level as the able-bodied employees.  The duty is
on the employer to take all steps short of undue hardship to accommodate the
needs of the person discriminated against so that they can compete equally with
the other employees.
It is by attempting to accommodate their actual
characteristics so as to bring them within the workplace environment that the
employer complies with the Code
. . . . (At para. 55, emphasis added.)

. . .

The appellant, in this case, does not seek
any reasonable accommodation or modification of the rule for the actual
characteristics of its disabled members.  Indeed, in this case, there is no
modification or accommodation possible.  The appellant asks, in effect, that
the rule as set out in the collective agreement be struck down. . . . (At para.
57.)

[
54
]                 This reasoning was endorsed and followed by the
Newfoundland Court of Appeal in
Power v. Canada
,
[1999] N.J. No. 30
(Q.L.)
(Nfld. S.C. Trial Div.)
, a case involving a federal government program
supporting the income of people who demonstrated an historical attachment to
fishery by tying compensation to the number of weeks worked at the fishery.
The Court held that this program does not contravene s. 15(1) of the
Charter

by treating employees who worked less time because of disability (and other)
absence from work unequally.  This judgment also discusses a number of other
recent decisions of the Federal Court of Canada.

[
55
]                 The Rasmussen Board sought to distinguish the Ontario
Court of Appeal’s decision in
Orillia Hospital
on the basis that the
Ontario legislation contains an express “BFOR” defence to the duty to
accommodate, not limited as the comparable defence in s. 16(7) in our
legislation appears to be, to the employer’s duty not to discriminate in
hiring.  In my view, this distinction is not significant. The duty to
accommodate the special characteristics of members of protected groups arises,
under our own legislation, not by virtue of an express legislative provision,
but by virtue of judicial implication, beginning with the decision of the
Supreme Court of Canada in
O’Malley
,
supra
.  There, and in
subsequent cases, the Court held that whether or not a provincial statute contains
either an express duty to accommodate differences or an express “BFOR” defence,
equality legislation implicitly prohibits not only direct discrimination, but
also “adverse impact” or “constructive” discrimination.  In cases where the
court finds adverse effect discrimination, however, (on a proper analysis
demonstrating that a rule or policy of general application, neutral on its
face, has a
disparate
effect on a complainant, identified by a protected
ground, in comparison with others in the appropriate comparator group), the
rule or policy is not struck down, but the court implies a duty to accommodate
the special needs of the complainant to the point of undue hardship.  The duty
to accommodate differences in cases of adverse effect discrimination is, therefore,
in an important sense, a judicially imposed duty, derived from a purposive
interpretation of human rights legislation.

[
56
]                 What the Ontario Court of Appeal has recognized, in
Orillia
Hospital
, is that comparisons in relation to compensation issues must be
made in recognition of the reality that normally the purpose or underlying
rationale of such benefits is to compensate employees for work performed.
Accordingly, to distinguish among employees on the basis of whether and to what
extent work has been performed does not contravene the equality principles
which drive the interpretation of legislation such as ours.  To say that the
duty to accommodate inherent in the Saskatchewan
Code
does not oblige
employers simply to top up wages of disabled employees who are unable, even
with full accommodation to the point of undue hardship, to perform work is
simply another way of saying the same thing.

[
57
]                 It is therefore my view that our own legislation, no
less than the Ontario legislation, requires consideration of the meaning of
adverse effect discrimination in the context of a reasonable interpretation of
what would be required to meet the duty to accommodate differences in treatment,
found on a comparative analysis that reflects the underlying rationale of the
rule or policy at issue,

in accordance with
the principles set out in
Gibbs
,
supra.
In this case, that analysis does not support the arbitrator’s
conclusion that the bonus provision of the collective agreement, as interpreted
by the Board, is discriminatory.  On the other hand, I would suggest, with
respect, that it is not possible to conclude, in light of the decisions of
the
Supreme Court of Canada in
Brooks
, Gibbs
and
Chambly,
that there
can
never
be an employer duty to accommodate the differences of disabled
persons in relation to issues of compensation, for this conclusion must depend
upon the outcome of the comparative analysis undertaken.

CONCLUSION

[
58
]                 For the reasons here set out, it is my conclusion
that the arbitration board erred in this case in its conclusion that the
provision of the collective bargaining agreement at issue contravenes
s. 16(1)

of
The
Saskatchewan Human Rights Code
.
That determination requires a
comparative analysis of the effect of the provision at issue in comparison with
the effect on other employees in an appropriate comparator group in light of
the underlying rationale of the benefit at issue.  That analysis does not in
this case lead to the conclusion that the provision at issue has an adverse
discriminatory impact on the grievor.

[
59
]                 The interim decision of the board is therefore
quashed.  The applicant shall have the costs of this application.
